title: Bad News: Humans Still Cant Multitask
author: Jared Cooney Horvath
summary: Jared Cooney Horvath debunks a wave of headlines claiming that new science has finally proven humans can multitask, arguing that the research actually confirms what cognitive scientists have known for decades: multitasking is only possible when one of the tasks has been automated through extensive practice. The new study demonstrates the phenomenon of automaticity — when a skill is mastered, the brain can run it in the background while conscious attention is directed elsewhere — which explains familiar examples like driving while singing or walking while talking. Horvath also explains the related concept of chunking, where two frequently co-practiced skills become neurologically bound into a single integrated routine, as with expert pianists coordinating both hands. Neither automaticity nor chunking creates a general-purpose multitasking capacity; they only permit concurrent performance of a practiced routine alongside a consciously attended task. The implications for classroom EdTech remain unchanged: students engaging with notifications, group chat, YouTube, and teacher instruction simultaneously are task-switching, not multitasking, and task-switching carries measurable cognitive costs in performance, memory, and reaction speed.
points: The 'new multitasking research' shows only that humans can perform two tasks simultaneously when one has been automated through practice — a finding confirmed by decades of prior science, not overturned by it.

Automaticity and chunking are real cognitive phenomena but strictly domain-specific: a pianist's coordinated hands do not transfer to general multitasking capacity any more than singing while driving means you can learn algebra while monitoring Snapchat.

Even automatic tasks are not immune to interference: being heavily absorbed in one task can impair performance of the supposedly-automated one, and beyond certain ages even basic dual tasks (walking and talking) show measurable interference.

The classroom implication is unambiguous: students cannot meaningfully learn algebra, monitor group chat, scan YouTube, answer notifications, and follow a teacher simultaneously — that activity is costly task-switching, regardless of what headlines claim.

Horvath's correction functions as a media-literacy lesson for educators: cognitive science headlines regularly overstate findings, and educators who defer to those headlines risk dismantling sound EdTech restrictions on false grounds.
quotes: The new study demonstrates something scientists have known for decades: humans can perform two tasks at once when one of those tasks has been practiced to the point of automaticity. In other words, when a skill has been mastered, the brain can largely run that skill in the background while conscious attention is directed elsewhere.

But this DOES NOT mean humans can develop some general, all-purpose multitasking capacity. It does not mean attention can magically expand — and it certainly does not negate the kind of media-multitasking encouraged by digital technologies (where novelty, interruption, and task-switching are the whole point).

When two or more skills are practiced together often enough, the brain can bind them into a single larger skillset. This is why novice pianists struggle to coordinate their left and right hands, while expert pianists can move both with ease: over time, the brain stops treating the hands as two separate tasks and begins treating them as one integrated act of 'playing piano.'
But again, chunking does not create a general ability to multitask. Rather, it compresses multiple component skills into a single practiced routine.

Students still cannot meaningfully learn algebra, monitor group chat, scan YouTube, answer notifications, and follow a teacher all at the same time. That remains task-switching — and task-switching remains costly.

Even when one task is a habitual routine, this does not guarantee effective multitasking. Rulesets, filters and goals can still become mixed up, leading to impaired reaction speed, performance and memory.
